Forget
fōr-GET
v. (rendering Hebrew shākach and Greek epilanthanomai)
From Old English forgietan, the prefix for- carrying a privative or destructive force (as in forbid, forsake) joined to gietan, to get or grasp — so, literally, to lose one's grip on. The Hebrew shākach is used the same way, of letting a thing slip out of mind and therefore out of practice, and the Greek epilanthanomai is built on lanthānō, to escape notice — what is forgotten has slipped past the attention.

Biblical Definition

Forgetting in Scripture is rarely a failure of the memory and almost always a failure of the heart. Moses warns Israel not against poor recall but against prosperity: “Beware that thou forget not the LORD thy God, in not keeping his commandments” (Deu 8:11) — and the verse defines the sin, because forgetting God is not keeping His commandments. The context makes the danger plain: when thou hast eaten and art full, and hast built goodly houses and dwelt therein, then thine heart be lifted up and thou forget. Judgment follows the category: “The wicked shall be turned into hell, and all the nations that forget God” (Psa 9:17) — not the nations that blaspheme Him, but simply those that leave Him out. Against this stands the impossibility of God's forgetting His own, put in the tenderest terms Scripture has: “Can a woman forget her sucking child?…yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee” (Isa 49:15), followed by the graving of Zion on the palms of His hands. And the writer to the Hebrews applies the same assurance to service: “God is not unrighteous to forget your work and labour of love” (Heb 6:10). There is also a forgetting that is commanded and holy — forgetting those things which are behind, Paul reaches forth unto those things which are before — and a forgetting that belongs to God alone, for He says of the new covenant that He will remember their sin no more.

Webster 1828 Definition

To lose from the mind, and in Scripture's idiom to lose from practice; the characteristic sin of the prosperous, defined by Moses as the not-keeping of God's commandments, and the one thing God declares He will not do toward His people or their labour of love.

expand to see more

FORGET, v.t. 1. To lose the remembrance of; to let go from the memory.

2. To slight; to neglect. Can a woman forget her sucking child? Isa. 49.

3. In Scripture, to forget God is to cease to regard his commandments and his benefits; a sin most incident to those in prosperity. Beware that thou forget not the LORD thy God. Deut. 8.

4. Of God, to forget is to withhold favor, or in mercy to remember sin no more. Their sin will I remember no more. Jer. 31.

5. To forget one's self; to lose the recollection of what belongs to one's character and station; and hence to be carried into unbecoming conduct.

Key Scripture

Deuteronomy 8:11 — "Beware that thou forget not the LORD thy God, in not keeping his commandments, and his judgments, and his statutes, which I command thee this day:"

Psalm 9:17 — "The wicked shall be turned into hell, and all the nations that forget God."

Isaiah 49:15 — "Can a woman forget her sucking child, that she should not have compassion on the son of her womb? yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee."

Hebrews 6:10 — "For God is not unrighteous to forget your work and labour of love, which ye have shewed toward his name, in that ye have ministered to the saints, and do minister."

Modern Corruption

Forgetting God is not treated as a sin at all in the modern conscience, since it involves no act; and where a nation quietly leaves God out of its reckoning, Psa 9:17 is precisely the verse being ignored.

expand to see more

Modern moral vocabulary is built almost entirely on acts and their consequences, which leaves it with no category for a sin of omission that feels like nothing. Yet Scripture names forgetting God as the road to judgment for whole nations, and Moses locates its cause not in hardship but in success: full barns, good houses, multiplied silver and gold, and then a lifted-up heart. A society may keep every outward decency and still be, in the exact sense of Psa 9:17, a nation that forgets God — and the mark of it is not open blasphemy but the quiet dropping of God from public reckoning as a subject that need not come up. Deu 8 makes the remedy as concrete as the danger: thou shalt remember the LORD thy God, for it is he that giveth thee power to get wealth.

There is also a therapeutic misuse of the biblical language of forgetting, which turns Paul's forgetting those things which are behind into a licence to bury sin without repentance and injury without reconciliation. Paul is describing the athlete's refusal to look back over his shoulder at attainments and failures alike while the race is still running; he is not counselling the suppression of what conscience has not dealt with. Scripture's way with the past is confession, restitution where it is owed, and forgiveness — after which the sin is genuinely gone, because God has said He will remember it no more. That is a divine act, not a technique, and no creature can perform it on himself.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shākach is to forget, mislay, or ignore. Greek epilanthanomai is to let escape notice, and lēthē, forgetfulness, gives 2Pe 1:9 its picture of a man who has forgotten that he was purged from his old sins.

expand to see more

Hebrew shākach (H7911) — to forget, to ignore, to cease to care for; some 102 occurrences, including the sheaf forgotten in the field and left for the stranger (Deu 24:19).

Hebrew nāshâh (H5382) — to forget, to deprive of memory; the root behind the name Manasseh, God hath made me forget all my toil (Gen 41:51).

Greek epilanthanomai (G1950) — to forget, to neglect; used in Heb 6:10 of what God will not do, and in Heb 13:2 and 16 of what we must not — hospitality, and to do good and communicate.

Greek lēthē (G3024) — forgetfulness; the noun in 2Pe 1:9, having forgotten that he was purged from his old sins.

Greek eklanthanomai (G1585) — to forget utterly, to let slip entirely; used once, in Heb 12:5, ye have forgotten the exhortation which speaketh unto you as unto children.

Usage

"Of the sin of the prosperous: beware that thou forget not the LORD thy God (Deu 8:11); when thy herds and thy flocks multiply, then thine heart be lifted up (Deu 8:13-14)."

"Of national judgment: all the nations that forget God (Psa 9:17); my people have forgotten me days without number (Jer 2:32)."

"Of what God will not forget and what He will: yet will I not forget thee (Isa 49:15); God is not unrighteous to forget your work (Heb 6:10); their sin will I remember no more (Jer 31:34)."
